title: Video Game Music
objective: After this level you can describe how game music grew from beeps to orchestras.
summary: Koji Kondo wrote Super Mario Bros. for three notes at once, with music that reacts to play. It became the first game music in the National Recording Registry in 2023.

cards.headline: In 2023, a video game tune joined America's archive of sound treasures.
cards.body: The Library of Congress added Koji Kondo's Super Mario Bros. theme, from 1985, to its National Recording Registry: the first video game music ever chosen. Not bad for music written for a very limited machine. Here's how game music got from beeps to that honor.

cards.headline: Three notes and a hiss
cards.body: Kondo later described what he had to work with: just three musical notes at a time, plus one white-noise sound, and very little data for music at all. Remember Level 1's harmony, notes sounding together? A single three-note chord would have used every voice the machine had. So every note had to earn its place, and Kondo made it sound effortless.

cards.headline: Music that plays along with you
cards.body: Film music follows a fixed story; game music has to follow you. Kondo wrote jingles to cheer players on after a Game Over, fanfares for reaching a goal, and pieces that sped up when time was running short. That last one is Level 4's tempo put to work: the clock is ticking, and the music makes sure you feel it.

mascot.line: Faster music, same game. Your pulse probably noticed before you did.

cards.headline: From sound chip to concert hall
cards.body: Those three-voice tunes didn't stay in the console. Kondo's Super Mario Bros. music has been performed by orchestras around the globe. And in 2023 the Grammys handed out their first award for video game scores, won by Stephanie Economou for Assassin's Creed Valhalla: Dawn of Ragnarok. Game music had graduated.

questions.prompt: Why was the Super Mario Bros. theme's 2023 entry into the National Recording Registry historic?

options.label: It was the oldest song ever added
options.rationale: It dates from 1985; plenty is older.

options.label: It won the Registry a Grammy
It was the first video game music chosen
It was the Registry's only instrumental
options.rationale: That isn't what made it historic.

questions.explanation: Koji Kondo's 1985 theme was the first video game music added to the Library of Congress National Recording Registry.

questions.prompt: Why did Koji Kondo have to be so inventive when writing the Super Mario Bros. music?

options.label: The machine offered three notes at once and little data
Nintendo banned melodies from its games
options.rationale: Melody was central to his music.

options.label: He had to record a live orchestra
options.rationale: The music came from the console's own sound.

options.label: Games then could not play music

questions.explanation: Kondo had just three musical notes at a time plus a noise sound, and very little data for music.

questions.prompt: When the Super Mario Bros. music speeds up as time runs short, which Level 4 idea is the game changing?

options.label: Tempo, the speed of the beat
Meter, how beats are grouped
options.rationale: The grouping isn't what speeds up.

options.label: Pitch, how high the notes are
options.rationale: Faster isn't the same as higher.

questions.explanation: Tempo is the speed of the beat, and Kondo's music sped up to make the ticking clock felt.
